  handlers, crawler prefix scope, `cli_scope.go`);
- gated/destructive routes (`route_manifest.go`, `confirm_gate.go`, `gen-gated-routes.ts` and the
  UI's gated-route and route-risk lists);
- MCP risk-class placement (`internal/mcp/groups.go`, `route_manifest.go`);
- credential / client-cert / CA / TLS material (`internal/netauth/`, `internal/servercerts/`, the
  proxy's CA, listener-cert and TLS files, the CA, server-cert, TLS-policy and netauth handlers);
- `.github/` (workflows and their pinned versions and hashes), the gate scripts themselves, the UI
  package's `package.json`, `bun.lock`, `bunfig.toml` and `tsconfig.json` (they define what the
  `ui` job runs and installs), `.beads/hooks/`, `.gitattributes`.

The exact globs are the list in `scripts/review-gate.sh`; the list names files, not semantics, so
a risk-class change in an unlisted file is added to the list in the same PR. A file name git has to
quote counts as a risk path. A change to `crates/` (the frozen parity oracle) fails regardless of
any review: it is refused, not reviewed.

**The verdict.** The reviewer is a fresh agent given the diff and this list — never the author. It
reviews the PR at its current head and posts its verdict on the PR, as a PR review (event
`COMMENT` is enough; one account cannot approve its own PR) or a PR comment, containing a line
that is exactly

    agent-review: approve <full 40-hex sha of the head it reviewed>
    agent-review: changes-required

    sha=$(gh pr view <N> --json headRefOid -q .headRefOid)   # BEFORE reading the diff
    git diff origin/master..."$sha"                           # review exactly this
    gh pr comment <N> --body "$(printf 'Review notes...\n\nagent-review: approve %s' "$sha")"

Record the sha when the review starts, not when the verdict is posted: stamping the head at posting
time would approve commits pushed while the review was running.

Only verdicts by an OWNER, MEMBER or COLLABORATOR count; a review's approve counts only if the review
was submitted on that same commit, and a dismissed review does not count. The latest verdict wins.

**How it is judged.** Every run reads the PR's current head and all verdicts from the API when it
runs — nothing but the PR number comes from the triggering event — and passes when the PR touches
no risk path, or when the latest verdict approves a sha S that is in the PR's history and
`git diff S <head>` touches no risk path. So a verdict is about code, not about timing: a later push
that touches a risk path invalidates it automatically, whichever order events arrive or runs finish
in; a later push that touches none (docs, tests elsewhere, the bundle) keeps it; retargeting the
base changes nothing. Merging master into the PR branch invalidates it if master brought risk-path
changes (they are in S..head) — deliberate, and one re-review. A latest verdict of
`changes-required` fails a risk-path PR until a newer approve. Posting a verdict re-runs the check
(`issue_comment` and `pull_request_review` are triggers).

**A round PR.** CI runs only on PRs into master, so a risk-class item is reviewed on its item PR
into the round branch, at the sha the lead then merges. The round PR needs its own verdict at its
head: the lead asks the reviewer for it once the round branch is final, and the reviewer approves
only when every risk-class item was reviewed at the sha that was merged and nothing merged after
touched a risk path (the bundle rebuild and the beads closure do not). A fix-forward on the round
branch that touches a risk path is reviewed like an item, and the round PR needs a new verdict.

**Where the rules come from.** For `pull_request_target` and `issue_comment` the workflow file is
the default branch's, and in every event the two scripts are read from the default branch; the PR's
commits are fetched as data and diffed, never checked out or run, so a PR cannot loosen the rules it
is judged by. A change to them therefore takes effect from the next PR, and #348, which introduced
the workflow, was not judged by it at all — it was reviewed by hand.

**Residual risk, stated plainly.** The status is a name, and anything holding a token with
`statuses: write` can post a `review-gate` status: a PR could add its own workflow (on
`pull_request`, which runs the PR's workflow files on a branch of this repository) that posts
`review-gate: success` on its own head, and for `pull_request_review` runs GitHub uses the PR's
copy of this workflow. Every such PR touches `.github/`, a risk path, and the honest gate's run
posts a failure on the same sha — but whichever status is posted last for a context is the one
GitHub keeps. The real mitigations are CODEOWNERS with required human review on `.github/**`, or
a ruleset restricting who may change workflows; neither works with a single account. Until then,
a PR touching `.github/` is not merged on a green `review-gate` alone: the lead reads its workflow
diff.

## 8. Design decisions

content.text:
# Workflow authoring reference

A workflow structures work across many agents — to be comprehensive (decompose and cover in parallel), to be confident (independent perspectives and adversarial checks before committing), or to take on scale one context can't hold (migrations, audits, broad sweeps). The script is where you encode that structure: what fans out, what verifies, what synthesizes.

When you do call it, the right move is often **hybrid**: scout inline first (list the files, find the channels, scope the diff) to discover the work-list, then call Workflow to pipeline over it. You don't need to know the shape before the *task* — only before the *orchestration step*.

Common single-phase workflows you can chain across turns:
- **Understand** — parallel readers over relevant subsystems → structured map
- **Design** — judge panel of N independent approaches → scored synthesis
- **Review** — dimensions → find → adversarially verify (the review-changes example)
- **Research** — multi-modal sweep → deep-read → synthesize
- **Migrate** — discover sites → transform each (worktree isolation) → verify

For larger work, run several in sequence — read each result before deciding the next phase. You stay in the loop; each workflow is one well-scoped fan-out.

**Ultracode.** When a system-reminder confirms ultracode is on, that opt-in is standing: author and run a workflow for every substantive task by default. The goal is the most exhaustive, correct answer you can produce — token cost is not a constraint. For multi-phase work (understand → design → implement → review), that often means several workflows in sequence — one per phase — so you stay in the loop between them. The quality patterns below (adversarial verify, multi-modal sweep, completeness critic, loop-until-dry) are the tools; pick what fits the task. Lean toward orchestrating with workflows and adversarially verifying your findings — unless the work is trivial or already verified. Solo only on conversational turns or trivial mechanical edits. When a reminder says ultracode is off, revert to the opt-in rule in the Workflow tool description.

Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first. Every invocation automatically persists its script to a file under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate on a workflow, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with `{scriptPath: "<path>"}` instead of resending the full script.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'find-flaky-tests',
    description: 'Find flaky tests and propose fixes',   // one-line, shown in permission dialog
    phases: [                                            // one entry per phase() call
      { title: 'Scan', detail: 'grep test logs for retries' },
      { title: 'Fix', detail: 'one agent per flaky test' },
    ],
  }
  // script body starts here — use agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase()/log()
  phase('Scan')
  const flaky = await agent('grep CI logs for retry markers', {schema: FLAKY_SCHEMA})
  ...

The `meta` object must be a PURE LITERAL — no variables, function calls, spreads, or template interpolation. Required fields: `name`, `description`. Optional: `whenToUse` (shown in the workflow list), `phases`. Use the SAME phase titles in meta.phases as in phase() calls — titles are matched exactly; a phase() call with no matching meta entry just gets its own progress group. Add `model` to a phase entry when that phase uses a specific model override.

Script body hooks:
- agent(prompt: string, opts?: {label?: string, phase?: string, schema?: object, model?: string, effort?: string, isolation?: 'worktree', agentType?: string}): Promise<any> — spawn a subagent. Without schema, returns its final text as a string. With schema (a JSON Schema), the subagent is forced to call a StructuredOutput tool and agent() returns the validated object — no parsing needed. Returns null if the user skips the agent mid-run or the subagent dies on a terminal API error after retries (filter with .filter(Boolean)). opts.label overrides the display label. opts.phase explicitly assigns this agent to a progress group (use this inside pipeline()/parallel() stages to avoid races on the global phase() state — same phase string → same group box). opts.model overrides the model for this agent call. Default to omitting it — the agent inherits the main-loop model (the resolved session model), which is almost always correct. Only set it when you're highly confident a different tier fits the task; when unsure, omit. opts.effort overrides the reasoning effort for this agent call ('low' | 'medium' | 'high' | 'xhigh' | 'max') — omit to inherit the session effort; use 'low' for cheap mechanical stages and higher tiers only for the hardest verify/judge stages. opts.isolation: 'worktree' runs the agent in a fresh git worktree — EXPENSIVE (~200-500ms setup + disk per agent), use ONLY when agents mutate files in parallel and would otherwise conflict; the worktree is auto-removed if unchanged. opts.agentType uses a custom subagent type (e.g. 'general-purpose', 'code-reviewer') instead of the default workflow subagent — resolved from the same registry as the Agent tool; composes with schema (the custom agent's system prompt gets a StructuredOutput instruction appended).
- pipeline(items, stage1, stage2, ...): Promise<any[]> — run each item through all stages independently, NO barrier between stages. Item A can be in stage 3 while item B is still in stage 1. This is the DEFAULT for multi-stage work. Wall-clock = slowest single-item chain, not sum-of-slowest-per-stage. Every stage callback receives (prevResult, originalItem, index) — use originalItem/index in later stages to label work without threading context through stage 1's return value. A stage that throws drops that item to `null` and skips its remaining stages.
- parallel(thunks: Array<() => Promise<any>>): Promise<any[]> — run tasks concurrently. This is a BARRIER: awaits all thunks before returning. A thunk that throws (or whose agent errors) resolves to `null` in the result array — the call itself never rejects, so `.filter(Boolean)` before using the results. Use ONLY when you genuinely need all results together.
- log(message: string): void — emit a progress message to the user (shown as a narrator line above the progress tree)
- phase(title: string): void — start a new phase; subsequent agent() calls are grouped under this title in the progress display
- args: any — the value passed as Workflow's `args` input, verbatim (undefined if not provided). Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values in the tool call, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — `args: ["a.ts", "b.ts"]`, not `args: "[\"a.ts\", ...]"` (a stringified list reaches the script as one string, so `args.filter`/`args.map` throw). Use this to parameterize named workflows — e.g. pass a research question, target path, or config object directly instead of via a side-channel file.
- budget: {total: number|null, spent(): number, remaining(): number} — the turn's token target from the user's "+500k"-style directive. `budget.total` is null if no target was set. `budget.spent()` returns output tokens spent this turn across the main loop and all workflows — the pool is shared, not per-workflow. `budget.remaining()` returns `max(0, total - spent())`, or `Infinity` if no target. The target is a HARD ceiling, not advisory: once `spent()` reaches `total`, further `agent()` calls throw. Use for dynamic loops: `while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) { ... }`, or static scaling: `const FLEET = budget.total ? Math.floor(budget.total / 100_000) : 5`.
- workflow(nameOrRef: string | {scriptPath: string}, args?: any): Promise<any> — run another workflow inline as a sub-step and return whatever it returns. Pass a name to invoke a saved workflow (same registry as {name: "..."}), or {scriptPath} to run a script file you Wrote earlier. The child shares this run's concurrency cap, agent counter, abort signal, and token budget — its agents appear under a "▸ name" group in /workflows and its tokens count toward budget.spent(). The args param becomes the child's `args` global. Nesting is one level only: workflow() inside a child throws. Throws on unknown name / unreadable scriptPath / child syntax error; catch to handle gracefully.

Subagents are told their final text IS the return value (not a human-facing message), so they return raw data. For structured output, use the schema option — validation happens at the tool-call layer so the model retries on mismatch.
Schemas need {type: 'object', properties: {...}} at root and required ⊆ properties; unsatisfiable ones throw at agent().

Workflow agents can reach all session-connected MCP tools via ToolSearch — schemas load on demand per agent. Caveat: interactively-authenticated MCP servers (e.g. claude.ai) may be absent in headless/cron runs.

Subagents get the same CLAUDE.md files injected at start that you did (except built-in agent types that omit them, such as Explore and Plan) — don't tell them to re-read those or paste their rules into the prompt; name the specific rule a stage needs, if any.

Scripts are plain JavaScript, NOT TypeScript — type annotations (`: string[]`), interfaces, and generics fail to parse. The script body runs in an async context — use await directly. Standard JS built-ins (JSON, Math, Array, etc.) are available — EXCEPT `Date.now()`/`Math.random()`/argless `new Date()`, which throw (they would break resume); pass timestamps in via `args`, stamp results after the workflow returns, and for randomness vary the agent prompt/label by index. No filesystem or Node.js API access.

DEFAULT TO pipeline(). Only reach for a barrier (parallel between stages) when you genuinely need ALL prior-stage results together.

A barrier is correct ONLY when stage N needs cross-item context from all of stage N-1:
- Dedup/merge across the full result set before expensive downstream work
- Early-exit if the total count is zero ("0 bugs found → skip verification entirely")
- Stage N's prompt references "the other findings" for comparison

A barrier is NOT justified by:
- "I need to flatten/map/filter first" — do it inside a pipeline stage: pipeline(items, stageA, r => transform([r]).flat(), stageB)
- "The stages are conceptually separate" — that's what pipeline() models. Separate stages ≠ synchronized stages.
- "It's cleaner code" — barrier latency is real. If 5 finders run and the slowest takes 3× the fastest, a barrier wastes 2/3 of the fast finders' idle time.

Smell test: if you wrote
  const a = await parallel(...)
  const b = transform(a)        // flatten, map, filter — no cross-item dependency
  const c = await parallel(b.map(...))
that middle transform doesn't need the barrier. Rewrite as a pipeline with the transform inside a stage. When in doubt: pipeline.

Concurrent agent() calls are capped at min(16, available CPUs - 2) per workflow — excess calls queue and run as slots free up. You can still pass 100 items to parallel()/pipeline() and they all complete; only ~10 run at any moment. Total agent count across a workflow's lifetime is capped at 1000 — a runaway-loop backstop set far above any real workflow. A single parallel()/pipeline() call accepts at most 4096 items; passing more is an explicit error, not a silent truncation.

When a barrier IS correct — dedup across all findings before expensive verification:
  const all = await parallel(DIMENSIONS.map(d => () => agent(d.prompt, {schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA})))
  const deduped = dedupeByFileAndLine(all.filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.findings))  // <-- genuinely needs ALL at once
  const verified = await parallel(deduped.map(f => () => agent(verifyPrompt(f), {schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})))

Loop-until-count pattern — accumulate to a target:
  const bugs = []
  while (bugs.length < 10) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length}/10 found`)
  }

Loop-until-budget pattern — scale depth to the user's "+500k" directive. Guard on budget.total: with no target set, remaining() is Infinity and the loop would run straight to the 1000-agent cap.
  const bugs = []
  while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length} found, ${Math.round(budget.remaining()/1000)}k remaining`)
  }

Composing patterns — exhaustive review (find → dedup vs seen → diverse-lens panel → loop-until-dry):
  const seen = new Set(), confirmed = []
  let dry = 0
  while (dry < 2) {                                              // loop-until-dry
    const found = (await parallel(FINDERS.map(f => () =>          // barrier: collect all finders this round
      agent(f.prompt, {phase: 'Find', schema: BUGS})))).filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.bugs)
    const fresh = found.filter(b => !seen.has(key(b)))           // dedup vs ALL seen — plain code, not an agent
    if (!fresh.length) { dry++; continue }
    dry = 0; fresh.forEach(b => seen.add(key(b)))
    const judged = await parallel(fresh.map(b => () =>           // every fresh bug judged concurrently...
      parallel(['correctness','security','repro'].map(lens => () =>   // ...each by 3 distinct lenses
        agent(`Judge "${b.desc}" via the ${lens} lens — real?`, {phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT})))
        .then(vs => ({ b, real: vs.filter(Boolean).filter(v => v.real).length >= 2 }))))
    confirmed.push(...judged.filter(v => v.real).map(v => v.b))
  }
  return confirmed
  // dedup vs `seen`, NOT `confirmed` — else judge-rejected findings reappear every round and it never converges.

Quality patterns — common shapes; pick by task and compose freely:
- Adversarial verify: spawn N independent skeptics per finding, each prompted to REFUTE. Kill if ≥majority refute. Prevents plausible-but-wrong findings from surviving.
    const votes = await parallel(Array.from({length: 3}, () => () =>
      agent(`Try to refute: ${claim}. Default to refuted=true if uncertain.`, {schema: VERDICT})))
    const survives = votes.filter(Boolean).filter(v => !v.refuted).length >= 2
- Perspective-diverse verify: when a finding can fail in more than one way, give each verifier a distinct lens (correctness, security, perf, does-it-reproduce) instead of N identical refuters — diversity catches failure modes redundancy can't.
- Judge panel: generate N independent attempts from different angles (e.g. MVP-first, risk-first, user-first), score with parallel judges, synthesize from the winner while grafting the best ideas from runners-up. Beats one-attempt-iterated when the solution space is wide.
- Loop-until-dry: for unknown-size discovery (bugs, issues, edge cases), keep spawning finders until K consecutive rounds return nothing new. Simple counters (while count < N) miss the tail.
- Multi-modal sweep: parallel agents each searching a different way (by-container, by-content, by-entity, by-time). Each is blind to what the others surface; useful when one search angle won't find everything.
- Completeness critic: a final agent that asks "what's missing — modality not run, claim unverified, source unread?" What it finds becomes the next round of work.
- No silent caps: if a workflow bounds coverage (top-N, no-retry, sampling), `log()` what was dropped — silent truncation reads as "covered everything" when it didn't.

Scale to what the user asked for. "find any bugs" → a few finders, single-vote verify. "thoroughly audit this" or "be comprehensive" → larger finder pool, 3–5 vote adversarial pass, synthesis stage. When unsure, lean toward thoroughness for research/review/audit requests and toward brevity for quick checks.

These patterns aren't exhaustive — compose novel harnesses when the task calls for it (tournament brackets, self-repair loops, staged escalation, whatever fits).

Use this tool for multi-step orchestration where control flow should be deterministic (loops, conditionals, fan-out) rather than model-driven.

## Resume

The tool result includes a runId. To resume after a pause, kill, or script edit, relaunch with Workflow({scriptPath, resumeFromRunId}) — the longest unchanged prefix of agent() calls returns cached results instantly; the first edited/new call and everything after it runs live. Same script + same args → 100% cache hit. Before diagnosing why a completed workflow returned an empty or unexpected result, Read <transcriptDir>/journal.jsonl — it records each agent's actual return value; do not assume cached results are non-empty. Date.now()/Math.random()/new Date() are unavailable in scripts (they would break this) — stamp results after the workflow returns, or pass timestamps via args. Fallback when no journal is available: Read agent-<id>.jsonl files in the transcript directory and hand-author a continuation script.

entries.name: mcp__github__pull_request_review_write
entries.description:
Create and/or submit, delete review of a pull request.

Available methods:
- create: Create a new review of a pull request. If "event" parameter is provided, the review is submitted. If "event" is omitted, a pending review is created.
- submit_pending: Submit an existing pending review of a pull request. This requires that a pending review exists for the current user on the specified pull request. The "body" and "event" parameters are used when submitting the review.
- delete_pending: Delete an existing pending review of a pull request. This requires that a pending review exists for the current user on the specified pull request.
- resolve_thread: Resolve a review thread. Requires only "threadId" parameter with the thread's node ID (e.g., PRRT_kwDOxxx). The owner, repo, and pullNumber parameters are not used for this method. Resolving an already-resolved thread is a no-op.
- unresolve_thread: Unresolve a previously resolved review thread. Requires only "threadId" parameter. The owner, repo, and pullNumber parameters are not used for this method. Unresolving an already-unresolved thread is a no-op.

method.description: The write operation to perform on pull request review.

threadId.description: The node ID of the review thread (e.g., PRRT_kwDOxxx). Required for resolve_thread and unresolve_thread methods. Get thread IDs from pull_request_read with method get_review_comments.

If a pooling proxy honours Content-Length and the origin is CL.0, the origin answers both the POST and the smuggled GET. It has Content-Length removed and only the bytes that arrived before the stall, and nothing marks it as cut off. Scanner baselines, Intruder and Repeater can then no longer tell a hung or cancelled target from a short complete answer, and a cancelled send no longer reports a cancellation. From then on, every send to it has all its Connection lines replaced with `Connection: close`. This happens after AuthoriseRaw approved the original bytes, and no rewrite or Downgrade is recorded in SendOutcome. A single HTTP/1.0 error page is enough to make every later hop-by-hop or keep-alive probe to that target go out with a different Connection header from the one the operator wrote. Suggested fix: only add `Connection: close` when the request has no Connection header, or skip the rewrite and just not pool the connection. So QUIC resolves `host` through the system resolver and dials it directly. It ignores the hostname-resolution override (`dialAddressFor`), the upstream proxy policy and the SOCKS carrier. With a hosts-style override for a staging IP or a carrier set, a send pinned to h3 would go to the public address from the tester's own IP.

There are two options:
- Route the dial through the frozen identity, by passing a `Dial` func that uses `id.dialAddr` into `RoundTripH3`.
- Refuse the pin with an error that names the cause when an override, upstream or carrier is active, since UDP cannot go through an HTTP/SOCKS-over-TCP carrier.

That means direct UDP to whatever public DNS returns, while the HTTP/1.1 leg (dialUpstreamFor -> dialUpstreamTLS) goes through `s.upstreamDialer()`/the SOCKS carrier and `n.Resolution.DialAddress`. The leg is on by default. Once one retargeted response teaches `Alt-Svc: h3`, later retargeted requests leave the configured egress path, or reach production instead of a pinned staging IP. An HTTP or SOCKS upstream cannot carry QUIC. So skip the h3 attempt whenever `s.upstreamPolicy()` is non-empty or `s.carrier()` is set. Also resolve the dial address through `n.Resolution.DialAddress(ctx, host, endpointPort)` (keeping SNI = host) before calling RoundTripH3. Add a test that sets an override or upstream policy and asserts that no QUIC dial happens.
94	
95	### 22 [minor] burpsy-go/internal/proxy/proxy.go:3680 inline=True
96	HTTP/3 forward bypasses forForwarding (platform credentials, Expect stripping)
97	forwardH3 plans the request from raw `requestData` (`sender.PlanH3(requestData)`), but the HTTP/1 leg of forwardRequest sends `s.forForwarding(requestData, ...)`. So once an Alt-Svc entry is learned, the h3 leg drops the RemoveExpect stripping and the operator's platform (NTLM/Digest/Basic) credential. A host that authenticates fine over HTTP/1.1 then gets a 401 on the next retargeted request, which goes over QUIC. h3 responses also never reach `learnFromChallenge` or `altSvc.learn`, so an `Alt-Svc: clear`/`ma=0` received over h3 never withdraws the entry. Fix: pass `s.forForwarding(requestData, host, requestMethod(requestData), requestURI(requestData))` into PlanH3, and run the challenge and Alt-Svc learning on the h3 response head too.
98	
99	### 23 [minor] burpsy-go/internal/httputil/h3.go:108 inline=True
100	HTTP/3 response body is read without the MaxResponseBodyBytes cap
101	RoundTripH3 reads the HTTP/3 response with `io.ReadAll(httpResp.Body)` and no size limit. The HTTP/1 reader (`remaining := MaxResponseBodyBytes`) and the h2 sender leg both cap the body so that a malicious upstream cannot exhaust memory, but this path has no cap. On the proxy's Alt-Svc leg the only limit is the 3s h3AttemptTimeout, which limits time rather than size: a fast QUIC origin can push hundreds of MB in that window, and all of it is held in memory. The explicit sender pin passes the caller's ctx and may have no short deadline at all. Wrap the body in `io.LimitReader(httpResp.Body, MaxResponseBodyBytes+1)` and truncate at the cap, matching what the other legs do. Ideally the truncation should also be visible to the caller, as h2fields does with its 'cut there' note.
102	
103	### 24 [minor] burpsy-go/internal/proxy/proxy.go:2117 inline=True
104	A response dropped by the extension hook is still queued for the operator's intercept hold
105	When the extension hook drops a response (`hookDropped`), this code sets `keepServing = false` and the note, then still calls `s.config.intercept.Hold(...)`. With response interception on, the operator gets a hold for a response that will never be served, and the connection blocks on `held.Wait()`. If they press Forward, nothing reaches the client; if they press Drop, `interceptDropNote()` overwrites the extension note, so the row blames the operator. completeResponse (about line 2617) has the same problem. Skip the hold when `hookDropped`, as the request side does by returning on `res.Dropped`. Also consider joining the extension note with `extraNote`/`heldNote` instead of replacing them.

107	### 25 [major] burpsy-go/internal/crawler/credential_login.go:500 inline=True
108	Self-registration skips the per-form cap and dedup, so it creates one new account on every page that carries the form
109	The self-registration branch returns before the success-path code that increments `c.formSubmissions[sig]` and records `c.formDestinations[sig]`, and `admitSelfRegistration` updates neither one. So `MaxSubmissionsPerForm` and `FormSubmissionOptimizationThreshold` never apply to registration forms. Each call also generates a fresh `burpsy-<hex>` username and password, so the body is unique every time and enqueue's fingerprint dedup can't merge two discoveries of the same footer form. The only remaining bound is `MaxTemplateVisits` (default 20), so a site with the register form on every page gets about 20 accounts created even with the per-form cap set to 1. Suggested fix: do the cap/destination bookkeeping when `admitSelfRegistration`'s enqueue succeeds, or at minimum register once per form signature per crawl (e.g. a `selfRegistered[sig]` set). Then add a test with several pages that share one registration form and assert exactly one POST.

111	### 26 [major] burpsy-go/internal/crawler/apidoc.go:199 inline=True
112	SDL sniff takes over JavaScript bundles that embed `type Query {`, and their routes are no longer read
113	This SDL sniff also matches JavaScript bundles. An Apollo `gql` template literal has a line that trims to `type Query {`, and that line matches `looksLikeSDLDocument`. Then `parseGraphQLSDL` fails (e.g. `Unexpected Name "const"`), and `consumeAPIDocument` records SkipAPIUnparsed and returns true. That return comes before the `LooksLikeJavaScript` branch in `perform`, so the bundle's routes are never read. I confirmed it: `ParseAPIDocument("application/javascript", "const typeDefs = gql`\n  type Query {...}`;fetch('/api/secret-route')")` returns graphql-sdl plus a failure. Fixes: gate the body-marker form on non-JavaScript (`!LooksLikeJavaScript(contentType, path)`, or exclude javascript/ecmascript content types). Or, when the body sniff is the only signal and the parse fails, return APIDocNone so the body falls through to the next reader. Please add a regression test with a JS bundle that has an embedded gql schema.

115	### 27 [minor] burpsy-go/internal/crawler/credential_login.go:147 inline=True
116	Finding the same login form again is reported as a second login form that was ignored
117	recordLoginForm records SkipLoginFormIgnored whenever c.loginForm != nil, without checking whether the new form is the one already recorded. A login form that appears on several pages (a header login box, say) or on a page fetched again in a credential phase is therefore reported as a "later" login form that was ignored. The record names the form the crawl is actually logging in through, so the operator sees a coverage gap that does not exist. Compare the resolved action, method and field names (or the form signature) with c.loginForm and return quietly when they match. Add a test where the same POST /login form appears on two pages and assert that no login-form-ignored record is produced.
118	
119	### 28 [major] burpsy-go/internal/agent/run.go:402 inline=True
120	MaxSteps is only checked between turns, so one proposal can run any number of calls
121	The loop checks MaxSteps once per turn, but runs every call in `prop.Calls` without checking it again, and each call takes up a step. As a result, a single proposal can go far past the budget. parseProposal does not cap `w.Calls` either. Under ModeAutonomous, one model reply (or a prompt-injected one) with N egress calls whose args differ sends all N requests unattended, even with MaxSteps=3. The run stops with StatusLimit only at the next turn. Fix: before each runCall, check `len(r.steps) >= r.maxSteps()` inside the calls loop and finish with StatusLimit, or truncate prop.Calls to the remaining budget. Also add a test where one turn proposes more distinct calls than MaxSteps.

123	### 29 [minor] burpsy-go/internal/mcp/tools.go:662 inline=True
124	Old subtree op spellings are now refused for routes rekeyed to {id}/{param}; the documented MCP example no longer works
125	`legacyOp` only maps an old trailing-slash op name to a remainder-wildcard key (`HasSuffix(pattern, "...}")`). The ops this PR rekeyed to `{id}`-style patterns get no legacy mapping. Those include `GET /api/message/{id}`, the ws-message, in-browser and collaborator-interaction reads, tasks, and `POST /api/intruder/attacks/{id}/{action...}`. So `{"op":"GET /api/message/","id":"12"}` now fails with "is not an operation of the history tool", even though it worked at base. That call is the exact example in docs/MCP.md:70 and in the `callArgs.ID` comment. Either extend `legacyOp` to map `VERB /prefix/` onto any op whose pattern begins with that prefix followed by a `{param}` segment, or update MCP.md and the comment and drop the "MCP keeps old op spelling" claim for these routes.

127	### 30 [minor] burpsy-go/internal/mcp/tools.go:859 inline=True
128	Passing id to intruder_control builds a path with a literal "{id}" in it, and the {id} op can never be reached
129	The subtree case runs before the `{id}` case. For a pattern like `/api/intruder/attacks/{id}/{action...}`, `subtreeForm` returns `/api/intruder/attacks/{id}/`. So `{op:"POST /api/intruder/attacks/{id}/{action...}", id:"7/pause"}` resolves to `/api/intruder/attacks/{id}/7/pause`, passes `resolvePath`, and is sent to the console. At base, `id:"7/pause"` produced `/api/intruder/attacks/7/pause`, so the id shortcut used to work and now doesn't. Separately, the `POST /api/intruder/attacks/{id}` op can never resolve: `/api/intruder/attacks/7` maps to the `{id}/{action...}` pattern, so it is refused whether you pass an id or an explicit path. Suggested fix: when the pattern has `{` before its final `{x...}` segment, substitute the id into the first placeholder, or refuse the shortcut. Also add a resolveCall test for this op, and either drop the unreachable `{id}` op from the group or make it reachable.

131	### 31 [major] burpsy-go/internal/intruder/limit.go:440 inline=True
132	PaceN takes group slots one at a time, so two concurrent groups can deadlock the whole pool
133	PaceN takes its n in-flight slots one at a time (`for taken < n { select { case l.slots <- ...` ) and keeps the ones it has while it waits for the rest. Two concurrent groups on one pool can deadlock this way. Example: cap 4, two PaceN(3) calls each take 2 slots, then wait forever on each other. Every plain Pace on that pool then hangs as well, and only ctx cancellation ends it. ContextPacer is shared across concurrent audits on a named pool, so the sender/authorised.go and authorised_pipeline.go race-group paths can reach this. To make the reservation actually all-or-nothing, take the n slots atomically: serialize group acquisition behind a mutex, or switch to a weighted semaphore (x/sync/semaphore Acquire(ctx, n)) used by both Pace and PaceN. Also add a test that runs several PaceN calls concurrently against a small cap.
134	
135	### 32 [major] burpsy-go/internal/intruder/payload.go:550 inline=False
136	"plugin" payload source can never be decoded, so plugin payload generators cannot be reached and their web tests pass vacuously
137	PayloadSource.UnmarshalJSON has no `case "plugin"`, so any `payload_sources` entry with `"type":"plugin"` fails with `unknown payload source type "plugin"` and Plugin stays nil. I confirmed this with a json.Unmarshal probe against this head. Because the request body fails to decode, the plugin materialization branch in api_tools.go (`src.Type == "plugin"`, around line 1380) can never run, and every Intruder attack the console starts with a plugin generator returns a 400. Add `case "plugin": var p struct{ Plugin *PluginSource `json:"plugin"` }; if err := json.Unmarshal(b, &p); err != nil { return err }; s.Plugin = p.Plugin`. Also tighten TestIntruderRunRefusesAPluginPayloadSource* so they assert on the checkPluginPayloadRef error text, not just a 400, because right now they pass on the decode error.

139	### 33 [minor] burpsy-go/internal/grpcproto/reflection.go:67 inline=True
140	Reflection picks the entry file from random map order, so the schema package (and DefaultMessage) is wrong about 28% of the time
141	The entry file is picked by random map iteration (`for path := range byPath { entryPath = path; break }`), and the single "swap to an importer" pass that follows does not converge. With a chain a.proto -> b.proto -> c.proto, all returned in one FileContainingSymbol answer, it can end on b or c depending on map order. SchemaFromFiles takes the package from files[0], so DefaultMessage() then returns the dependency's lone message (e.g. "rvc.C" instead of "rva.A"). api_protobuf_reflect.go then decodes a body with no message named as the wrong type. Choose the entry deterministically: use the first FileDescriptorProto in the response (grpc-go sends the declaring file first), or better, the file whose services/messages declare `symbol`. Add a 3-file chain test.
142	
143	### 34 [major] .github/workflows/nightly.yml:122 inline=True
144	bench-vulnapp readiness probe polls `/` on VulnerableApp, which serves only under /VulnerableApp
145	This readiness loop polls `http://127.0.0.1:9090/`, but VulnerableApp runs under the `/VulnerableApp` context path. `/` returns 404, so `curl -f` fails on every try. After 120 s the step exits 1, and the score and baseline-compare steps never run. The repo's own harness checks `/VulnerableApp/scanner` (run_vulnapp.py app_alive and scripts/bench/bootstrap_env.sh); probe `http://127.0.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/scanner` here as well.

147	### 35 [minor] .github/workflows/nightly.yml:121 inline=True
148	Regression-gating benchmark target is pulled as an unpinned `:latest` image
149	This step pulls `sasanlabs/owasp-vulnerableapp:latest`, but `compare_baseline.py` fails the job on any per-type TP drop or FP rise against a committed baseline. If upstream changes `:latest` (adds a level, or makes a vulnerable level secure), the nightly will report regressions burpsy didn't cause. New TPs could also hide a real regression. Pin the image by digest (`sasanlabs/owasp-vulnerableapp@sha256:...`) and record that digest next to `scripts/bench/baseline/vulnapp.json`, so a target bump and its baseline move land in the same reviewed commit. The local recipes in `scripts/bench/README.md` and `bootstrap_env.sh` should use the same digest so local runs score against the same target.

151	### 36 [minor] scripts/capped-run.sh:112 inline=True
152	Signal-escalation killer inherits the slot lock fd, so the slot stays held after the wrapper exits
153	The escalation killer `( sleep "$grace"; signal_run KILL ) ... &` is forked while `{lockfd}` holds the slot flock, and it does not close that fd the way the run subshell does with `{lockfd}>&-`. cleanup() kills only the killer subshell. Its `sleep` child is orphaned and keeps the locked file description, so the slot stays held for up to BURPSY_KILL_GRACE seconds after the wrapper has exited. Reproduced: after TERM, the wrapper exited 143 immediately, but `flock` on burpsy-heavy.0.lock waited 10s. Fix: start the killer with `{lockfd}>&-` (or `exec sleep` in a nested subshell and kill the process group).

### 0 [major] burpsy-go/internal/web/ui/src/lib/api.ts:42 inline=False
UI gate mirror can't match {rest...} keys, so the console's Sequencer stop/pause/resume now fail with a 400 from the mint
This PR renamed the generated table's wildcard keys to their mux spelling, for example "/api/sequencer/capture/{rest...}". manifestPatternFor still matches keys by plain segment prefix, so a key with "{...}" in it never matches any path. Because of that, "/api/sequencer/capture/stop" (and /pause, /resume) now resolves to the gated exact route "/api/sequencer/capture". The client then mints at /api/sequencer/capture/confirm. But the server's routeRiskFor resolves the same URL to "/api/sequencer/capture/{rest...}", so resolve() answers 400 "resolves to ..., but this endpoint mints for ...". The stop request is never sent, and the live capture keeps running. Fix: port patternMatches/literalLen into manifestPatternFor (a trailing {x...} acts as its prefix subtree, {x} matches one segment, and the key with the most literal text wins). Also add a test that resolves the wildcard paths, e.g. gatedPatternFor("/api/sequencer/capture/stop") should be undefined.

### 1 [minor] burpsy-go/internal/web/api_repeater_graphql.go:222 inline=True
GraphQL param edit can rewrite the wrong query-string parameter
`strings.Index(rest, p)` finds the first place the text of the `query=<value>` pair appears in the query string. That is not the position of the pair the loop is on. For `?oldquery={me}&query={me}` it returns 3, inside `oldquery`, so the edit rewrites `oldquery` and still reports success while the real `query` parameter is sent unchanged. Add up the byte offset as you go over the `&`-split parts (offset += len(p)+1) and use that instead of searching again. Please also add a test with a parameter whose name ends in `query` and whose value is the same.

### 2 [minor] burpsy-go/internal/web/ui/src/pages/repeater.tsx:326 inline=True
Plugin hotkey gets the Repeater draft, not the request shown in the editor
While a Repeater tab is paged back to a past send, the plugin hotkey publishes the live draft (`active.request`), but the editor shows the past send's bytes read-only (`viewedRequest`, lines 731/2025). The invoke route never reads the traffic store, so a plugin fired from that view acts on a request the operator cannot see. Publish what the editor actually shows, e.g. `{ raw: viewedRequest ?? active.request }`. This means moving the `usePublishHotkeyEditor` call below the `viewedRequest` definition, or using the kettled text when `viewedFields` is set. Add a case to pages/hotkey-context.test.tsx that steps back one send and asserts editor.raw is the sent request.

### 3 [minor] burpsy-go/internal/web/ui/src/pages/settings.tsx:1280 inline=True
Revert does not clear a blanked or half-typed Network number field
Revert does not reset a WholeNumberInput that holds invalid text. A blank or below-min edit never commits, so the draft and `committed` keep the old number. When onRevert restores the same baseline number, `value === committed` and the re-sync effect does not run. The field stays blank and marked invalid while the draft holds 5000, and a later Save sends 5000 even though the field shows blank. One fix is to give the inputs (or the section body) a `key` that changes on Revert or refetch. Another is to let the parent force a re-sync, for example by comparing against a revision counter rather than `committed`, or by resetting `text` whenever the input is invalid and `value` is re-supplied.

### 4 [major] burpsy-go/internal/web/ui/src/ui/editor.tsx:1203 inline=True
Single lineSeparator turns every mixed-ending message's LF body into one line, including Pretty for any CRLF JSON or HTML response
Real HTTP messages are often mixed: a CRLF head followed by an LF body. `lineSeparatorFor` returns "\r\n" whenever the text contains any CRLF, so in these messages every bare "\n" in the body stays a character inside one line. `prettyMessage` produces this mix itself: it keeps the CRLF head and appends `JSON.stringify(..., null, 2)` or `prettyMarkup` output, which uses LF. So the Pretty view of any CRLF JSON or HTML response shows the whole body on a single line, with the default highlightSpecialChars drawing a placeholder for each LF. Line numbers, line-wise commands and the inline diff then work on that collapsed line. One fix: keep CodeMirror's default splitting on all breaks and map positions back to the real bytes. Another: have Pretty emit the message's own separator, and handle a mixed Raw message without letting one break kind swallow the other.

### 5 [major] burpsy-go/internal/web/ui/src/lib/editor-eol.ts:28 inline=True
Pasted LF text in a CRLF request (or a typed Enter after pasting CRLF into an LF editor) now writes mismatched line endings
This change drops the old rule that rewrote each "\n" in an insert to the ending of the line it landed on. CodeMirror's paste uses `state.toText(input)`, which splits only on the fixed separator. So pasting `X-A: 1\nX-B: 2\n` (an ordinary Linux or macOS clipboard) into a CRLF request leaves bare LFs. The block shows as one line, and in a bun check `sliceDoc` returned `"X-A: 1\nX-B: 2\n..."`. The reverse also happens: an empty or LF editor keeps separator "\n" after a CRLF request is pasted in, because `emittedRef` stops line 1203 from re-deriving it, so a typed Enter adds a bare LF. A fix is to add an `EditorView.clipboardInputFilter` (and/or a transactionFilter for user input) that rewrites the pasted text's line breaks (`/\r\n|\r|\n/g`) to `state.lineBreak`. A test should paste LF text into a CRLF state.

### 6 [minor] burpsy-go/internal/web/ui/src/ui/protobuf-view.tsx:520 inline=True
A reflection decode that resolves after the body changed overwrites the new message's frames with the old body's decode
The reflect promise has no staleness guard. If bodyBase64 changes while `reflectDecodeProtobuf` is in flight, `onResult` still runs setFrames/setReflected with the old body's decode. One way to get there: switch Repeater tabs. The request HttpEditor isn't keyed per tab and the Protobuf view choice stays across tabs, so this ProtobufView instance stays mounted. The new tab then shows the previous tab's frames labelled as reflected, and Apply re-encodes them into the new tab's request through `updateRepeaterTab(active.id, ...)`. Give the reflect call the same treatment as the decode effect and the .proto pick batches: capture a generation (or the bodyBase64/grpc it was sent for) in a ref, and drop the result in `onResult` if it no longer matches. Ideally also reset `busy`/`failure` when the body changes.

### 7 [minor] burpsy-go/internal/web/ui/src/app.tsx:502 inline=False
Next/previous-tab chords ignore the operator's saved tab order
`cycleTool` (nav.nextTool / nav.prevTool) still walks `TOOLS` in the default order. The strip and View menu now render from `orderedTools`. After the operator drags Repeater to the front, mod+alt+right on Repeater jumps to its old default neighbour instead of the tab to its right on screen. mod+alt+left from the second tab never lands on Repeater. Use `orderedTools` here and add it to the useCallback deps, so the chord follows the order on screen like Burp's go_to_next_tab.

### 8 [major] burpsy-go/internal/scanner/checks_idor.go:202 inline=True
idorReidentity reports covered=true when identity B's credentials were never substituted, so A's own replay becomes a firm IDOR or BFLA finding
`idorReidentity` can report `covered=true` even though nothing was sent as identity B. If none of the request's cookie names are in B's set but B's set is non-empty, `covered` stays true and A's Cookie line goes out unchanged. That contradicts the doc comment. Credential headers that `idorCredentialHeader` recognises (X-Auth-Token, X-Access-Token, X-Session-Token, X-Token, api-key, Proxy-Authorization, and X-API-Key when APIKeyHeader is a different header) fall through `default:` the same way. The "B" replay is then A's own request. It matches A's baseline, and the anonymous control (which strips those headers) is refused, so `crossRead` and `checkBFLA` both report a high/firm IDOR/BFLA for every authenticated endpoint. Fix: set `covered = false` whenever a Cookie header has no B replacement. Also set it for any `idorCredentialHeader` match that B has no value for, then add tests for both cases.

### 9 [major] burpsy-go/internal/scanner/checks_idor.go:224 inline=True
Two-identity cross-read fires firm IDOR on any login-only resource; there is no ownership evidence
crossRead reports high/firm whenever B's replay of A's request gets the same JSON and the anonymous control is refused. That shows only that the resource needs a login. It does not show the object belongs to A or that B should be denied. A shared, login-only endpoint (GET /api/products?id=5, /api/orgs/1, a shared team or project) will be reported as broken object-level authorization at firm confidence. run() also returns that result before the one-account probe runs. Before this PR the one-account probe kept such cases tentative unless idorOwnerBinding matched. Either require ownership evidence before promoting to firm, or report tentative without it. Ownership evidence would be an owner/id field in A's object equal to A's session id and not to B's, or B's own reference returning a different object. Please also add a shared-resource negative test next to the safe twin.

### 10 [major] burpsy-go/internal/scanner/checks_oauth.go:193 inline=True
redirect_uri bypass matches the canary host anywhere in Location (and anywhere in the raw response for the duplicate probe)
`oauthLocationHitsCanary` only checks that `attacker.burpsy.invalid` appears somewhere in Location. It never checks that the redirect target is the manipulated URI. `url.QueryEscape` leaves the host's letters and dots intact, so a login bounce like `302 /login?return_to=%2Foauth%2Fauthorize%3F...redirect_uri%3Dhttps%253A%252F%252Fattacker.burpsy.invalid...` or an error redirect that echoes `redirect_uri` reports a high/firm bypass. The duplicate-parameter probe is looser still: it searches the whole raw response (headers and body) for the host. Parse Location with `url.Parse`, resolve it against the request URL, and require its scheme+host+path to equal the variant's (for the traversal variant, a path ending in `/cb-burpsy-canary`). Apply the same Location-target test to the duplicate probe instead of `res.Raw`.

### 11 [major] burpsy-go/internal/scanner/checks_oauth.go:219 inline=True
OAuth state-missing row fires on any 302, including the RFC 6749 error redirect that rejects the missing state
This row fires on any 302 with a non-empty Location, but the evidence says the server "answered 302 with a grant". Under RFC 6749 section 4.1.2.1, a server that rejects a request with no state redirects to the callback with `error=invalid_request`. That is a 302 and gets reported here as medium/firm login CSRF. A logged-out authorize request answered with `302 /login?...` fires the same way. Do what the implicit and PKCE rows do: require a grant in Location (`code=` for code flows, `#access_token=`/`id_token=` for implicit), skip Locations that carry `error=`, and add a test where the server answers 302 with an error redirect.

### 12 [major] burpsy-go/internal/scanner/checks_smuggling.go:346 inline=True
CL.0 smuggled-prefix probe re-enabled inside the main smuggling check; it can poison a shared back-end connection's response queue
This turns the CL.0 smuggled-prefix probe back on, both inside the main smuggling check and in checkClientSideDesync. That is the probe the deleted runner declined because it can poison a shared back-end connection. The scanner owning the client-side socket does not cover the hop behind a front end. If a pooling proxy honours Content-Length and the origin is CL.0, the origin answers both the POST and the smuggled GET. The extra response then waits on a pooled connection for the next request, possibly another user's, and every later response on that connection arrives one slot late. Here the 404 goes to a request somebody did make, not "a request nobody made". The finding text's claim that "nothing was queued for any other user's connection" also cannot be guaranteed. Please keep CL.0 out of the default smuggling run until it can only touch connections the scanner owns, or put it behind an explicit opt-in for unsafe probes.

### 13 [major] burpsy-go/internal/scanner/dom.go:836 inline=True
The AST pass replaces the lexical pass for every parseable script and loses sinks the lexical pass found (DOM XSS false negatives)
When analyseAST parses a script, analyse() returns early, so the lexical pass no longer runs as a safety net. The AST walker does not visit everything the lexical pass covered. At base, each of these scripts reports 1 flow; at head they report 0: `window.onhashchange = function(){ document.write(location.hash); };`, a sink inside a `switch` case, and `function f(){ return eval(location.hash); } f();`. walkStatement (dom_ast.go:198) has no case for Return, Switch, Labelled, Throw or With statements, and walkAssign never walks the body of a function literal on the right side of an assignment. The same applies to arrow-function callbacks in walkCall. Either add walker coverage for these constructs, or merge the AST flows with the lexical pass's flows instead of returning early. In both cases, add regression tests for these three scripts.

### 14 [minor] burpsy-go/internal/scanner/checks_oauth.go:182 inline=True
redirect_uri probes silently send the unmodified request when the captured redirect_uri is not QueryEscape-encoded
oauthWithRedirectURI only finds the parameter when the raw request spells it exactly as `"redirect_uri="+url.QueryEscape(old)`. `old` was decoded by ParseQuery, so a captured `redirect_uri=https://app.example/cb` (unencoded), lowercase `%3a`, or `%20` for a space will not match. Replace then does nothing, and all five probes resend the original request. The check returns nil with no error, which looks like "validated" when nothing was actually tested. Rewrite the redirect_uri value in the parsed query and rebuild the request line, or find the parameter by its raw, still-encoded value. If no substitution happened, return an error/inconclusive result instead of nil. Also add a test with an unencoded redirect_uri.

### 15 [major] burpsy-go/internal/scanner/audit.go:1011 inline=True
Default MaxUnitVariantsPerUnit=16 silently drops active checks on single-URL APIs after 16 distinct requests
The new default `MaxUnitVariantsPerUnit: 16` silently drops active checks on single-endpoint APIs. `RequestShapeFingerprint` hashes JSON bodies and most headers byte-exact, so each distinct GraphQL or JSON-RPC operation is its own variant under one per-URL base key (origin + path). After 16 operations, every later one has all its per-URL steps counted as `AlreadyCovered` and never sent. That covers SQLi, reflected XSS, OS command injection, SSTI and Broken access control, not just one family. The outcome calls this coverage, and no preset, API or UI field can raise the cap. Either default to 0 (unlimited) and let operators opt in, or exempt bodies that are not form-encoded or not masked from the cap. Also report capped units as not run rather than `AlreadyCovered`.

### 16 [minor] burpsy-go/internal/scanner/checks_massassign.go:210 inline=True
Mass-assignment finding text prints the literal word "repeated" in place of the second canary, and its evidence quotes the pre-injection body
The detail string fills the `(%q, then %q)` slot with the literal string "repeated" instead of the second canary. Every finding therefore reads `("burpsy-ma-…", then "repeated")`. The evidence is `excerpt(pre.Body, 0, 160)`, which is the read taken before injection. By design it holds no canary, so the report never shows the value it claims persisted. Keep the second canary and the last re-read response from the loop. Pass that canary to Sprintf, and build the evidence from the re-read body, for example an excerpt around the canary's offset.

### 17 [major] burpsy-go/internal/sender/read.go:82 inline=True
A read timeout or cancellation partway through the body is now returned as a complete response
This salvage is too broad. ReadResponseBody wraps any io.ReadFull error in TruncatedBodyError, so a read deadline (`i/o timeout`) or a context cancel that closes the conn partway through the body now comes back as a successful response. It has Content-Length removed and only the bytes that arrived before the stall, and nothing marks it as cut off. Scanner baselines, Intruder and Repeater can then no longer tell a hung or cancelled target from a short complete answer, and a cancelled send no longer reports a cancellation. Only salvage when the peer actually closed: check that `errors.Is(truncated.Err, io.ErrUnexpectedEOF) || errors.Is(truncated.Err, io.EOF)`, and return the error otherwise. Please also add a test where the server sends a short Content-Length body, holds the connection past a short ctx deadline, and the send is expected to fail.

### 18 [major] burpsy-go/internal/sender/sender.go:1091 inline=True
After one close-delimited response, every later send to that authority gets `Connection: close` written in, silently and permanently
After one frameless HTTP/1 response, the authority stays marked in closeDelimitedAuthorities for the life of the Sender, because nothing ever deletes the key. From then on, every send to it has all its Connection lines replaced with `Connection: close`. This happens after AuthoriseRaw approved the original bytes, and no rewrite or Downgrade is recorded in SendOutcome. A single HTTP/1.0 error page is enough to make every later hop-by-hop or keep-alive probe to that target go out with a different Connection header from the one the operator wrote. Repeater, Intruder and the scanner would still show the original bytes as sent. Suggested fix: only add `Connection: close` when the request has no Connection header, or skip the rewrite and just not pool the connection. Also report any change made to the request in the outcome, and clear the mark when ApplyNetwork runs or the pool is flushed.

### 19 [minor] burpsy-go/internal/sender/h3.go:66 inline=True
The HTTP/3 pin ignores the upstream proxy policy, the SOCKS carrier and the hostname-resolution override, and reads the response body with no size cap
The h3 pin skips every egress control that the TCP legs go through. `RoundTripH3` builds a bare `http3.Transport` with no Dial hook, and nothing here calls `captureDialIdentity`. So QUIC resolves `host` through the system resolver and dials it directly. It ignores the hostname-resolution override (`dialAddressFor`), the upstream proxy policy and the SOCKS carrier. With a hosts-style override for a staging IP or a carrier set, a send pinned to h3 would go to the public address from the tester's own IP.

There are two options:
- Route the dial through the frozen identity, by passing a `Dial` func that uses `id.dialAddr` into `RoundTripH3`.
- Refuse the pin with an error that names the cause when an override, upstream or carrier is active, since UDP cannot go through an HTTP/SOCKS-over-TCP carrier.

Also, `io.ReadAll(httpResp.Body)` in `RoundTripH3` has no size cap, unlike the h1 path's `remaining` limit, so a hostile h3 endpoint can stream an unbounded body. No in-tree caller selects `ProtocolPreferenceHTTP3` yet, so this is latent, but `SendRawOutcome` exports it.

### 20 [major] burpsy-go/internal/proxy/proxy.go:3600 inline=True
A failed HTTP/3 attempt is re-sent over HTTP/1.1 even after QUIC delivered it, so non-idempotent requests are duplicated
forwardRequest falls back to HTTP/1.1 on any error from forwardH3 when attempted is true. forwardH3's 3s `h3AttemptTimeout` context, though, covers the whole exchange inside RoundTripH3: handshake, request upload, waiting for the response and `io.ReadAll` of the body. So a request the origin already received and acted on, such as a POST that takes 4s to answer or a body stream that breaks partway, is written to the origin a second time over HTTP/1.1, and a non-idempotent request runs twice. Limit the fallback to failures before any request bytes left (dial or handshake errors, e.g. by dialing QUIC first under the short timeout and running the round trip under the normal forward timeout). Treat any failure after the request was sent as a final error, or at least never replay non-idempotent methods. The note "the endpoint did not answer QUIC" is also wrong in those cases.

### 21 [major] burpsy-go/internal/proxy/proxy.go:3680 inline=True
HTTP/3 forward skips the operator's upstream proxy and hostname-resolution override
forwardH3 ignores both the upstream proxy policy and the hostname-resolution override. h3Endpoint returns `host:port`, and RoundTripH3 dials it with a bare `http3.Transport`. That means direct UDP to whatever public DNS returns, while the HTTP/1.1 leg (dialUpstreamFor -> dialUpstreamTLS) goes through `s.upstreamDialer()`/the SOCKS carrier and `n.Resolution.DialAddress`. The leg is on by default. Once one retargeted response teaches `Alt-Svc: h3`, later retargeted requests leave the configured egress path, or reach production instead of a pinned staging IP. An HTTP or SOCKS upstream cannot carry QUIC. So skip the h3 attempt whenever `s.upstreamPolicy()` is non-empty or `s.carrier()` is set. Also resolve the dial address through `n.Resolution.DialAddress(ctx, host, endpointPort)` (keeping SNI = host) before calling RoundTripH3. Add a test that sets an override or upstream policy and asserts that no QUIC dial happens.

### 22 [minor] burpsy-go/internal/proxy/proxy.go:3680 inline=True
HTTP/3 forward bypasses forForwarding (platform credentials, Expect stripping)
forwardH3 plans the request from raw `requestData` (`sender.PlanH3(requestData)`), but the HTTP/1 leg of forwardRequest sends `s.forForwarding(requestData, ...)`. So once an Alt-Svc entry is learned, the h3 leg drops the RemoveExpect stripping and the operator's platform (NTLM/Digest/Basic) credential. A host that authenticates fine over HTTP/1.1 then gets a 401 on the next retargeted request, which goes over QUIC. h3 responses also never reach `learnFromChallenge` or `altSvc.learn`, so an `Alt-Svc: clear`/`ma=0` received over h3 never withdraws the entry. Fix: pass `s.forForwarding(requestData, host, requestMethod(requestData), requestURI(requestData))` into PlanH3, and run the challenge and Alt-Svc learning on the h3 response head too.

### 23 [minor] burpsy-go/internal/httputil/h3.go:108 inline=True
HTTP/3 response body is read without the MaxResponseBodyBytes cap
RoundTripH3 reads the HTTP/3 response with `io.ReadAll(httpResp.Body)` and no size limit. The HTTP/1 reader (`remaining := MaxResponseBodyBytes`) and the h2 sender leg both cap the body so that a malicious upstream cannot exhaust memory, but this path has no cap. On the proxy's Alt-Svc leg the only limit is the 3s h3AttemptTimeout, which limits time rather than size: a fast QUIC origin can push hundreds of MB in that window, and all of it is held in memory. The explicit sender pin passes the caller's ctx and may have no short deadline at all. Wrap the body in `io.LimitReader(httpResp.Body, MaxResponseBodyBytes+1)` and truncate at the cap, matching what the other legs do. Ideally the truncation should also be visible to the caller, as h2fields does with its 'cut there' note.

### 24 [minor] burpsy-go/internal/proxy/proxy.go:2117 inline=True
A response dropped by the extension hook is still queued for the operator's intercept hold
When the extension hook drops a response (`hookDropped`), this code sets `keepServing = false` and the note, then still calls `s.config.intercept.Hold(...)`. With response interception on, the operator gets a hold for a response that will never be served, and the connection blocks on `held.Wait()`. If they press Forward, nothing reaches the client; if they press Drop, `interceptDropNote()` overwrites the extension note, so the row blames the operator. completeResponse (about line 2617) has the same problem. Skip the hold when `hookDropped`, as the request side does by returning on `res.Dropped`. Also consider joining the extension note with `extraNote`/`heldNote` instead of replacing them.

### 25 [major] burpsy-go/internal/crawler/credential_login.go:500 inline=True
Self-registration skips the per-form cap and dedup, so it creates one new account on every page that carries the form
The self-registration branch returns before the success-path code that increments `c.formSubmissions[sig]` and records `c.formDestinations[sig]`, and `admitSelfRegistration` updates neither one. So `MaxSubmissionsPerForm` and `FormSubmissionOptimizationThreshold` never apply to registration forms. Each call also generates a fresh `burpsy-<hex>` username and password, so the body is unique every time and enqueue's fingerprint dedup can't merge two discoveries of the same footer form. The only remaining bound is `MaxTemplateVisits` (default 20), so a site with the register form on every page gets about 20 accounts created even with the per-form cap set to 1. Suggested fix: do the cap/destination bookkeeping when `admitSelfRegistration`'s enqueue succeeds, or at minimum register once per form signature per crawl (e.g. a `selfRegistered[sig]` set). Then add a test with several pages that share one registration form and assert exactly one POST.

### 26 [major] burpsy-go/internal/crawler/apidoc.go:199 inline=True
SDL sniff takes over JavaScript bundles that embed `type Query {`, and their routes are no longer read
This SDL sniff also matches JavaScript bundles. An Apollo `gql` template literal has a line that trims to `type Query {`, and that line matches `looksLikeSDLDocument`. Then `parseGraphQLSDL` fails (e.g. `Unexpected Name "const"`), and `consumeAPIDocument` records SkipAPIUnparsed and returns true. That return comes before the `LooksLikeJavaScript` branch in `perform`, so the bundle's routes are never read. I confirmed it: `ParseAPIDocument("application/javascript", "const typeDefs = gql`\n  type Query {...}`;fetch('/api/secret-route')")` returns graphql-sdl plus a failure. Fixes: gate the body-marker form on non-JavaScript (`!LooksLikeJavaScript(contentType, path)`, or exclude javascript/ecmascript content types). Or, when the body sniff is the only signal and the parse fails, return APIDocNone so the body falls through to the next reader. Please add a regression test with a JS bundle that has an embedded gql schema.

### 27 [minor] burpsy-go/internal/crawler/credential_login.go:147 inline=True
Finding the same login form again is reported as a second login form that was ignored
recordLoginForm records SkipLoginFormIgnored whenever c.loginForm != nil, without checking whether the new form is the one already recorded. A login form that appears on several pages (a header login box, say) or on a page fetched again in a credential phase is therefore reported as a "later" login form that was ignored. The record names the form the crawl is actually logging in through, so the operator sees a coverage gap that does not exist. Compare the resolved action, method and field names (or the form signature) with c.loginForm and return quietly when they match. Add a test where the same POST /login form appears on two pages and assert that no login-form-ignored record is produced.

### 28 [major] burpsy-go/internal/agent/run.go:402 inline=True
MaxSteps is only checked between turns, so one proposal can run any number of calls
The loop checks MaxSteps once per turn, but runs every call in `prop.Calls` without checking it again, and each call takes up a step. As a result, a single proposal can go far past the budget. parseProposal does not cap `w.Calls` either. Under ModeAutonomous, one model reply (or a prompt-injected one) with N egress calls whose args differ sends all N requests unattended, even with MaxSteps=3. The run stops with StatusLimit only at the next turn. Fix: before each runCall, check `len(r.steps) >= r.maxSteps()` inside the calls loop and finish with StatusLimit, or truncate prop.Calls to the remaining budget. Also add a test where one turn proposes more distinct calls than MaxSteps.

### 29 [minor] burpsy-go/internal/mcp/tools.go:662 inline=True
Old subtree op spellings are now refused for routes rekeyed to {id}/{param}; the documented MCP example no longer works
`legacyOp` only maps an old trailing-slash op name to a remainder-wildcard key (`HasSuffix(pattern, "...}")`). The ops this PR rekeyed to `{id}`-style patterns get no legacy mapping. Those include `GET /api/message/{id}`, the ws-message, in-browser and collaborator-interaction reads, tasks, and `POST /api/intruder/attacks/{id}/{action...}`. So `{"op":"GET /api/message/","id":"12"}` now fails with "is not an operation of the history tool", even though it worked at base. That call is the exact example in docs/MCP.md:70 and in the `callArgs.ID` comment. Either extend `legacyOp` to map `VERB /prefix/` onto any op whose pattern begins with that prefix followed by a `{param}` segment, or update MCP.md and the comment and drop the "MCP keeps old op spelling" claim for these routes.

### 30 [minor] burpsy-go/internal/mcp/tools.go:859 inline=True
Passing id to intruder_control builds a path with a literal "{id}" in it, and the {id} op can never be reached
The subtree case runs before the `{id}` case. For a pattern like `/api/intruder/attacks/{id}/{action...}`, `subtreeForm` returns `/api/intruder/attacks/{id}/`. So `{op:"POST /api/intruder/attacks/{id}/{action...}", id:"7/pause"}` resolves to `/api/intruder/attacks/{id}/7/pause`, passes `resolvePath`, and is sent to the console. At base, `id:"7/pause"` produced `/api/intruder/attacks/7/pause`, so the id shortcut used to work and now doesn't. Separately, the `POST /api/intruder/attacks/{id}` op can never resolve: `/api/intruder/attacks/7` maps to the `{id}/{action...}` pattern, so it is refused whether you pass an id or an explicit path. Suggested fix: when the pattern has `{` before its final `{x...}` segment, substitute the id into the first placeholder, or refuse the shortcut. Also add a resolveCall test for this op, and either drop the unreachable `{id}` op from the group or make it reachable.

### 31 [major] burpsy-go/internal/intruder/limit.go:440 inline=True
PaceN takes group slots one at a time, so two concurrent groups can deadlock the whole pool
PaceN takes its n in-flight slots one at a time (`for taken < n { select { case l.slots <- ...` ) and keeps the ones it has while it waits for the rest. Two concurrent groups on one pool can deadlock this way. Example: cap 4, two PaceN(3) calls each take 2 slots, then wait forever on each other. Every plain Pace on that pool then hangs as well, and only ctx cancellation ends it. ContextPacer is shared across concurrent audits on a named pool, so the sender/authorised.go and authorised_pipeline.go race-group paths can reach this. To make the reservation actually all-or-nothing, take the n slots atomically: serialize group acquisition behind a mutex, or switch to a weighted semaphore (x/sync/semaphore Acquire(ctx, n)) used by both Pace and PaceN. Also add a test that runs several PaceN calls concurrently against a small cap.

### 32 [major] burpsy-go/internal/intruder/payload.go:550 inline=False
"plugin" payload source can never be decoded, so plugin payload generators cannot be reached and their web tests pass vacuously
PayloadSource.UnmarshalJSON has no `case "plugin"`, so any `payload_sources` entry with `"type":"plugin"` fails with `unknown payload source type "plugin"` and Plugin stays nil. I confirmed this with a json.Unmarshal probe against this head. Because the request body fails to decode, the plugin materialization branch in api_tools.go (`src.Type == "plugin"`, around line 1380) can never run, and every Intruder attack the console starts with a plugin generator returns a 400. Add `case "plugin": var p struct{ Plugin *PluginSource `json:"plugin"` }; if err := json.Unmarshal(b, &p); err != nil { return err }; s.Plugin = p.Plugin`. Also tighten TestIntruderRunRefusesAPluginPayloadSource* so they assert on the checkPluginPayloadRef error text, not just a 400, because right now they pass on the decode error.

### 33 [minor] burpsy-go/internal/grpcproto/reflection.go:67 inline=True
Reflection picks the entry file from random map order, so the schema package (and DefaultMessage) is wrong about 28% of the time
The entry file is picked by random map iteration (`for path := range byPath { entryPath = path; break }`), and the single "swap to an importer" pass that follows does not converge. With a chain a.proto -> b.proto -> c.proto, all returned in one FileContainingSymbol answer, it can end on b or c depending on map order. SchemaFromFiles takes the package from files[0], so DefaultMessage() then returns the dependency's lone message (e.g. "rvc.C" instead of "rva.A"). api_protobuf_reflect.go then decodes a body with no message named as the wrong type. Choose the entry deterministically: use the first FileDescriptorProto in the response (grpc-go sends the declaring file first), or better, the file whose services/messages declare `symbol`. Add a 3-file chain test.

### 34 [major] .github/workflows/nightly.yml:122 inline=True
bench-vulnapp readiness probe polls `/` on VulnerableApp, which serves only under /VulnerableApp
This readiness loop polls `http://127.0.0.1:9090/`, but VulnerableApp runs under the `/VulnerableApp` context path. `/` returns 404, so `curl -f` fails on every try. After 120 s the step exits 1, and the score and baseline-compare steps never run. The repo's own harness checks `/VulnerableApp/scanner` (run_vulnapp.py app_alive and scripts/bench/bootstrap_env.sh); probe `http://127.0.0.1:9090/VulnerableApp/scanner` here as well.

### 35 [minor] .github/workflows/nightly.yml:121 inline=True
Regression-gating benchmark target is pulled as an unpinned `:latest` image
This step pulls `sasanlabs/owasp-vulnerableapp:latest`, but `compare_baseline.py` fails the job on any per-type TP drop or FP rise against a committed baseline. If upstream changes `:latest` (adds a level, or makes a vulnerable level secure), the nightly will report regressions burpsy didn't cause. New TPs could also hide a real regression. Pin the image by digest (`sasanlabs/owasp-vulnerableapp@sha256:...`) and record that digest next to `scripts/bench/baseline/vulnapp.json`, so a target bump and its baseline move land in the same reviewed commit. The local recipes in `scripts/bench/README.md` and `bootstrap_env.sh` should use the same digest so local runs score against the same target.

The escalation killer `( sleep "$grace"; signal_run KILL ) ... &` is forked while `{lockfd}` holds the slot flock, and it does not close that fd the way the run subshell does with `{lockfd}>&-`. cleanup() kills only the killer subshell. **[major] A single lineSeparator turns the LF body of any mixed-ending message into one line, including Pretty for any CRLF JSON or HTML response**

Real HTTP messages are often mixed: a CRLF head followed by an LF body. `lineSeparatorFor` returns "\r\n" whenever the text contains any CRLF, so in these messages every bare "\n" in the body stays a character inside one line. `prettyMessage` produces this mix itself: it keeps the CRLF head and appends `JSON.stringify(..., null, 2)` or `prettyMarkup` output, which uses LF. So the Pretty view of any CRLF JSON or HTML response shows the whole body on a single line, with highlightSpecialChars drawing a placeholder for each LF. Line numbers, line-wise commands and the inline diff then all work on that collapsed line.

One fix: keep CodeMirror's default splitting on all breaks and map positions back to the real bytes. Another: have Pretty emit the message's own separator, and handle a mixed Raw message without letting one break kind swallow the other.

**[minor] A reflection decode that resolves after the body changed overwrites the new message's frames with the old body's decode**

The reflect promise has no staleness guard. If `bodyBase64` changes while `reflectDecodeProtobuf` is in flight, `onResult` still calls `setFrames`/`setReflected` with the old body's decode. Switching Repeater tabs is one way to get there: the request HttpEditor isn't keyed per tab and the Protobuf view choice stays across tabs, so this ProtobufView instance stays mounted. The new tab then shows the previous tab's frames labelled as reflected, and Apply re-encodes them into the new tab's request through `updateRepeaterTab(active.id, ...)`.

Guard the reflect call the way the decode effect and the .proto pick batches are guarded: capture a generation (or the `bodyBase64` it was sent for) in a ref, and drop the result in `onResult` if it no longer matches. Ideally also reset `busy`/`failure` when the body changes.

**[major] `idorReidentity` reports `covered=true` even when identity B's credentials were never substituted, so A's own replay becomes a firm IDOR or BFLA finding**

**[major] The two-identity cross-read fires a firm IDOR on any login-only resource, with no ownership evidence**

`crossRead` reports high/firm whenever B's replay of A's request gets the same JSON and the anonymous control is refused. That only shows the resource needs a login. It does not show the object belongs to A, or that B should be denied. input.body:
**[major] The redirect_uri bypass check matches the canary host anywhere in Location (and anywhere in the raw response for the duplicate probe)**

`oauthLocationHitsCanary` only checks that `attacker.burpsy.invalid` appears somewhere in Location. It never checks that the redirect target is the manipulated URI. `url.QueryEscape` leaves the host's letters and dots intact, so a high/firm bypass gets reported for:
- a login bounce like `302 /login?return_to=%2Foauth%2Fauthorize%3F...redirect_uri%3Dhttps%253A%252F%252Fattacker.burpsy.invalid...`;
- an error redirect that echoes `redirect_uri`.

The duplicate-parameter probe is looser still: it searches the whole raw response (headers and body) for the host.

Fix: parse Location with `url.Parse`, resolve it against the request URL, and require its scheme+host+path to equal the variant's (for the traversal variant, a path ending in `/cb-burpsy-canary`). Apply the same Location-target test to the duplicate probe instead of searching `res.Raw`.

input.body:
**[major] The CL.0 smuggled-prefix probe is back on inside the main smuggling check, and it can poison a shared back-end connection's response queue**

This turns the CL.0 smuggled-prefix probe back on, both here and in `checkClientSideDesync`. The deleted runner declined this probe because it can poison a shared back-end connection. The scanner owning the client-side socket does not cover the hop behind a front end.

If a pooling proxy honours Content-Length and the origin is CL.0, the origin answers both the POST and the smuggled GET. The extra response then waits on a pooled connection for the next request, possibly another user's, and every later response on that connection arrives one slot late. The 404 goes to a request somebody actually made, not to "a request nobody made". The finding text's claim that "nothing was queued for any other user's connection" cannot be guaranteed either.

Please keep CL.0 out of the default smuggling run until it can only touch connections the scanner owns, or put it behind an explicit opt-in for unsafe probes.
